passage: Layla had said something cutting to Diego at the party in Buenos Aires, about him always being late, and he had left early. For three days there was silence. She rehearsed a hundred messages. Finally she wrote, "Diego, what I said at the party was unkind. I was stressed and took it out on you, and that was my part. I'm sorry. I'd like to hear how it felt for you, whenever you're ready, no rush." He didn't reply that day. On the fifth day he wrote, "I was really hurt. Can we walk on Sunday?" Layla replied yes, and on the walk she mostly listened, without demanding that things go back to how they were.

qa.q: In which city was the party?
qa.a: The party was in Buenos Aires.

qa.q: What does Layla's message suggest she feels about her part in the fallout?
qa.a: Layla said she was stressed and took it out on Diego, and that her words were unkind. She did not blame him or demand forgiveness.

qa.q: What could Layla do on the walk?
qa.a: Listen to how it felt for Diego, avoid excuses and let Diego decide how fast things repair.

qa.q: How might Diego have felt in the days of silence?
qa.a: Diego was probably hurt and needed time, since he wrote on the fifth day that he was really hurt and asked to walk.

grounding: A young adult reaches out after a fallout, names their part, listens and does not demand instant forgiveness.

passage: In the staffroom of the primary school, Mehak and Sonali had stopped talking after an argument about the timetable, in which Mehak had accused Sonali of being lazy. Days later, in the corridor by the notice board, Mehak said, "Sonali, can I say something? What I said about you being lazy was unfair. I was frustrated, and I blamed you instead of asking. I'm sorry." Sonali crossed her arms and looked away. "I need a bit of time," she said. Mehak's stomach dropped, but she nodded. "Of course. I'm here when you want to talk." Two days later Sonali brought her a cup of tea, and they finally talked it out.

qa.q: Where did Mehak apologise to Sonali?
qa.a: Mehak apologised in the corridor by the notice board.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when she crossed her arms?
qa.a: Sonali was probably still hurt or guarded, and asked for a bit of time. Mehak accepted this without pushing.

qa.q: What did Mehak do well in her apology?
qa.a: She named exactly what was unfair, said why without excusing it, and accepted Sonali's need for time.

qa.q: How might Mehak have felt when Sonali asked for time?
qa.a: Mehak probably felt worried and disappointed, as her stomach dropped, but she respected the request and said she was there when Sonali wanted to talk.

grounding: A young adult reaches out after a fallout, names their part, listens and gives the other person time.

passage:
Kashish,
It's been three weeks since the fight at Ria's birthday, and I've started this message ten times.
I want to say clearly what I did. I told everyone about your breakup when you'd asked me to keep it private. I did it to seem like I knew things. That was wrong, and I'm sorry. Not "sorry if you felt hurt." Just sorry.
I'd like to hear your side, all of it, even the angry parts. When you're ready. If that's in a day, or a month, I'll wait. I'm not asking you to forgive me in your reply, or to reply at all.
I miss you. I miss our Sunday momos. But I understand if you need time.
Bidisha

qa.q: How long has it been since the fight?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: What is Bidisha feeling while writing?
qa.a: Bidisha feels guilty and nervous, having started the message ten times, and misses Kashish.

qa.q: What makes Bidisha's message a good repair attempt?
qa.a: It names Bidisha's part clearly, apologises without excuses, offers to listen, and does not demand quick forgiveness.

qa.q: What might Kashish need before replying?
qa.a: Kashish may need time to process the betrayal, and Bidisha's message leaves space for that.

grounding: Shows a young adult reaching out after a fallout, naming their part, offering to listen and not demanding instant forgiveness.

passage: Pema, you asked on your podcast how I got my best friend back. I'm Tarun, and it's not a pretty story. Last year Aman and I fell out badly. I'd promised to help him move flat, and I just didn't show up. I went to a cricket match instead. Didn't even text. He called me selfish, I called him dramatic, and we stopped talking. For a month I told myself he was overreacting. Then I realised I'd have been furious too. So I called him. He didn't pick up. I sent a message: "I skipped your move for a match and didn't tell you. That was selfish. I'm sorry. I'd like to hear how it was for you, whenever you're ready." Nothing for a week. I didn't push. Then he texted: "Chai Sunday?" He talked; I listened. He was still angry. That was okay. We're good now.

qa.q: What did Tarun go to instead of helping Aman move?
qa.a: A cricket match.

qa.q: How did Aman feel about Tarun not showing up?
qa.a: He felt let down and angry, calling Tarun selfish, and was still angry when they finally met.

qa.q: What did Tarun do right when he reached out?
qa.a: Tarun named what happened, called it selfish, apologised, offered to listen, and didn't push when Aman took a week to reply.

qa.q: What would change if Tarun had demanded an answer right away?
qa.a: Aman might have felt pressured and pulled further away instead of choosing to meet in his own time.

grounding: Shows a young adult repairing a friendship by naming their part, listening and respecting the other's timing.

passage: I'm Vandana, and I share a flat with Tejas, so I saw the whole thing. He and Kunal had fought over a group project. Tejas had taken credit in front of the professor for a chart Kunal made. Kunal stopped coming over. For two weeks Tejas sulked, saying Kunal was being "sensitive". Then one evening I saw him sitting on the balcony, phone in hand, typing and deleting. He finally sent something. The next day Kunal came to the door. Tejas didn't start with excuses. I heard him say, "I took credit for your chart. That was wrong. I told the professor this morning it was yours." Kunal didn't smile. He said, "I'm still angry." Tejas said, "That's okay. I'll wait." Kunal left after ten minutes. I don't know what Tejas felt; he just made two cups of tea and drank both. A week later, Kunal was back on our sofa.

qa.q: What did Tejas take credit for?
qa.a: A chart Kunal made.

qa.q: What might Kunal have been feeling when he said "I'm still angry"?
qa.a: He was still hurt and angry about the stolen credit, even though Tejas had apologised and corrected it.

qa.q: What did Tejas do that made repair possible?
qa.a: He named his part without excuses, told the professor the truth, and accepted that Kunal needed time.

qa.q: How does Vandana see the change in Tejas?
qa.a: Vandana saw him move from sulking and blaming Kunal to owning his mistake, though Vandana can't be sure what he felt.

grounding: Shows through an observer a young adult repairing a rupture by naming his part and respecting the other's timing.

passage:
Sunday: Two days after the party, Jasleen typed and deleted for an hour, then sent: "I told everyone about your crush on Kunal and turned it into a joke. That was my fault, and I'm sorry. You don't have to reply." No reply came. Jasleen checked her phone every ten minutes, then made herself stop.
Thursday: Reena passed her in the library and gave a small nod, nothing more. Jasleen's stomach dropped, but she didn't chase after her. That night a message arrived: "Got your text. I'm still angry. Need some time." Jasleen answered: "Okay. I'll be here when you're ready."
Two weeks later: Reena sat down across from her at the canteen. "It wasn't just the crush," she said. "It felt like my secrets were entertainment." Jasleen didn't defend herself. She listened, then said, "You're right. I wanted the laugh more than I protected you." Reena pushed half her samosa across the table.

qa.q: What did Jasleen reveal at the party?
qa.a: Reena's crush on Kunal.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel while waiting for a reply?
qa.a: Jasleen felt anxious and guilty, checking the phone every ten minutes but making herself stop so as not to pressure Reena.

qa.q: What helped repair the friendship?
qa.a: Jasleen named her own part without excuses, didn't demand forgiveness, gave Reena time, and listened without defending herself.

qa.q: What was the rupture like for Reena?
qa.a: It felt as if her secrets were entertainment, so she stayed angry and needed two weeks before she could talk.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult repairing a friendship by naming their part, giving the other person days of space, and listening without demanding forgiveness.
